Physics Lab 2

Rust & Metal

Give the wrecking ball real materials: rust that grows out of noise, steel, concrete and dust, then light it and render it.

Start the lab

Rendered in Blender by following the steps in this lab.

Today

We are learning

how real surfaces are described with three dials, how two materials can share one object through a mask, and why a render never looks like the viewport until you light it.

You need Blender 4.3 or newer (4.2 works with one substitution in the troubleshooting list), your Lab 1 file or the start file in Step 1, and a mouse with a scroll wheel. This lab takes about two lessons. Save your file as PhysicsLab2_RustMetal_YourName.blend.

You’ve got it when you can

  • set Base Color, Metallic and Roughness and say what each does
  • blend two shaders with a Mix Shader
  • add and wire nodes in the Shader Editor
  • turn a Noise Texture into a sharp mask with a Color Ramp
  • edit a shared material and read its user count
  • light a scene with a world colour and a sun, render and save a PNG

The plan

Five parts. Each one ends with a rendered picture of what your scene should look like.

  1. Part 1Open the sceneSteps 1–2
  2. Part 2Two shaders, one ballSteps 3–6
  3. Part 3Where the rust goesSteps 7–11
  4. Part 4Concrete, steel, dustSteps 12–14
  5. Part 5Light it and render itSteps 15–18

Materials are recipes, not paint

A material in Blender is a little program that answers one question for every point on a surface: what happens to light that hits here? Base Color says what colour bounces back, Metallic says whether the reflection is tinted like metal or white like paint, Roughness says how blurred the reflection is. Those three dials, done with real physics (PBR: physically based rendering), describe almost everything.

The ball needs two answers at once: steel here, rust there. A Mix Shader holds both recipes and a mask decides which one wins at each point. The mask grows out of a Noise Texture cut into black and white by a Color Ramp. And because a render only has the light you give it, the last part is lighting.

Word bank — open this if a word in the steps is new
Material
The recipe for how a surface reacts to light. Objects point at a material; several can share one.
Shader / BSDF
The part of the recipe that does the light maths. Principled BSDF does everything; Metallic BSDF does only metal.
Base Color
The surface’s own colour, typed as a Hex code like 8B3A1A.
Metallic
0 for paint, plastic, rust, concrete; 1 for metal. Rarely in between.
Roughness
0 = mirror, 1 = chalk. How blurred the reflections are.
IOR
Index of refraction. Leave it at 1.5 unless you are making glass or water.
Mix Shader
A node that blends two shaders. Factor 0 = all the first, 1 = all the second.
Node
A box in the Shader Editor. Sockets on the left take inputs, sockets on the right give outputs; wires join them.
Noise Texture
A node that makes a smooth random cloud of values from 0 to 1. Scale = how many blobs; Detail = how wrinkly.
Color Ramp
A node that maps incoming values (0 to 1) to colours along a bar. With black and white stops close together it makes a hard mask.
Mask
A black-and-white picture that says where something applies. White = yes.
Material Preview
Viewport shading that shows materials under a built-in studio light. Not what renders.
World
The sky around the scene: a colour (or sky texture) that lights everything softly and is what shiny things reflect.
Sun light
Parallel light from one direction, same strength everywhere. Strength about 3 for daylight.
Render
Computing the final picture (F12). Image › Save As keeps it.

Part 1

Open the scene

Tools: File › Open, Save As, Numpad 0, the Material Preview button.

This lab paints the wrecking ball scene from Physics Lab 1. Nothing moves: the physics is already baked. All the work is in materials, which is why it fits in two lessons.

The three dials

Pick a colour, drag Metallic and Roughness, watch the ball.

How the steps work

Each step has a Where line (which part of the Blender window to look at), a Watch animation of the mouse doing the step (pause it, drag the slider, or use the arrow buttons to go one move at a time), and a Do this list of the same moves as a, b, c. Do one move, look at the animation, do the next. The drawings are simplified, not screenshots: the words and positions match Blender, the exact colours and spacing may not.

  1. Open Lab 1, save it as Lab 2

    The File menu at the very top-left.

    Do this:

    1. a
      File › Open. Find PhysicsLab1_WreckingBall_YourName.blend and open it. No Lab 1 file? Download the start file (the finished Lab 1 scene, already baked) and open that.
    2. b
      File › Save As. Type PhysicsLab2_RustMetal_YourName and click Save Blender File. Your Lab 1 file stays as it was.

    You should now see: the chain, ball, wall and ground from Lab 1, and the new file name in the window title.

    Why not just keep working in the Lab 1 file?

    Because Lab 1 is marked separately and because materials experiments go wrong. Save As gives you a copy to break. The physics bake comes with the copy, so nothing needs re-simulating.

  2. Camera view, Material Preview

    The viewport, and the four shading spheres at its top-right.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Hover the viewport, press Numpad 0: the camera view. Stay on frame 1 (the raised chain) for now: the ball is easy to see there.
    2. b
      Top-right of the viewport: four small spheres. Click the third one, Material Preview. (Or press Z and pick it from the pie.)

    You should now see: the scene with colour and shine: a dark ball, grey links, sandy blocks, lit by a soft studio light that is built into this view.

    What is Material Preview?

    Solid shading shows shapes in flat grey. Material Preview shows every material as it will look, lit by a built-in studio light. It is for working on materials. Rendered shading (the fourth sphere) uses your own lights instead; Part 5 comes back to that.

End of Part 1. Save.

Part 2

Two shaders, one ball

Tools: the Material tab, the Surface dropdown, Mix Shader, Hex colours.

Rusty steel is two materials at once: steel where the paint held, rust where it did not. So the ball gets two shaders, a metal one and a rust one, and a Mix Shader that blends them. In this part the blend is a plain 50/50 everywhere; Part 3 turns it into patches.

  1. The Ball’s second slot

    The viewport, then the Material tab (red ball icon) in the Properties editor.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Click the Ball. Material tab. The slot list at the top shows Steel and Iron: the Ball is one object with two materials, because in Lab 1 it was joined from a link and a sphere.
    2. b
      Click the Iron slot (the sphere). Click the name box below the list, type RustySteel, Enter.

    You should now see: the second slot now reads RustySteel; the panel below shows Surface: Principled BSDF with a dark Base Color.

    Why two slots?

    Ctrl+J in Lab 1 kept both materials: the link’s Steel and the sphere’s Iron, each still assigned to its own faces. Edit the wrong slot and you would be painting the eye, not the ball. The eye stays plain steel; the sphere gets the rust.

  2. Surface: Mix Shader

    Material tab › Surface panel › the Surface dropdown.

    Do this:

    1. a
      The Surface dropdown says Principled BSDF. Click it and pick Mix Shader.

    You should now see: the panel changes to Factor 0.500 and two rows that both say Shader: None. The ball turns black.

    Black?

    A Mix Shader blends whatever is plugged into its two Shader slots. Both are empty, so it blends nothing with nothing: black. The next two steps fill them.

  3. First shader: steel

    The first Shader row under Mix Shader.

    Do this:

    1. a
      First Shader row › Metallic BSDF. Its own settings appear underneath, indented.
    2. b
      Click its Base Color swatch › Hex tab › type 3A3A3A. Click away to close the picker.
    3. c
      Roughness: 0.65.

    You should now see: a dull dark-grey ball: half steel, half nothing.

    Metallic BSDF or Principled BSDF?

    Metallic BSDF is a shader that is only ever metal, so it has no Metallic slider. Principled BSDF can be anything (paint, skin, glass, metal) and has every slider. For the steel half either works; Metallic BSDF keeps the panel short. It arrived in Blender 4.3; on an older Blender use Principled BSDF with Metallic 1.0 instead.

  4. Second shader: rust, and the Factor

    The second Shader row, then the Factor box.

    Predict first: Rust is not metallic and is very rough. Which two numbers in the Principled BSDF say that?

    Do this:

    1. a
      Second Shader row › Principled BSDF. Base Color Hex 8B3A1A. Metallic 0. Roughness 0.85.
    2. b
      Look at the ball: an even brown everywhere. Factor is the mix: type 0 (all steel), then 1 (all rust), then back to 0.5.

    You should now see: the ball switching between dark steel, orange rust and the brown halfway mix. Leave it at 0.5.

    What does Factor mean?

    Factor 0 means 100% of the first shader; Factor 1 means 100% of the second; 0.5 is half each at every point on the surface. One number for the whole ball is why it looks like brown paint. Rust is patchy: some points need Factor 0 and others Factor 1. That is a mask, and it is Part 3.

End of Part 2. Save.

Part 3

Where the rust goes

Tools: the Shading workspace, the Shader Editor, Shift+A, dragging wires, the Color Ramp.

A mask is a black-and-white picture that says where something goes: white here means rust here. Blender can grow one out of pure randomness: a Noise Texture makes a smooth cloud of greys, and a Color Ramp cuts the cloud into black and white. Wire that into the Mix Shader’s Factor and the ball rusts in patches.

Noise, ramp, mask

The three pictures are the three nodes. Drag the stops to cut the cloud.

  1. The Shading workspace

    The workspace tabs along the very top of the window.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Click the Shading tab at the top. The window rearranges: a viewport above, the Shader Editor below.
    2. b
      Hover the Shader Editor and press Home so every node fits. Scroll to zoom, middle-drag (or Alt + left-drag) to pan.

    You should now see: four boxes joined by green wires: Metallic BSDF and Principled BSDF going into Mix Shader, going into Material Output.

    Is this a different material?

    No: it is the same RustySteel, drawn as a graph. Every row you set in the Properties editor is a socket on one of these nodes, and the Surface dropdown was choosing what plugs into Material Output. The graph view can do one thing the panel cannot: plug a texture into a number.

  2. A Noise Texture

    The Shader Editor. Shift+A, then click to place.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Hover the Shader Editor. Shift+A › Texture › Noise Texture. The node sticks to the mouse: move it to the empty space left of the shaders and click.
    2. b
      In the node: Scale 6, Detail 4, Roughness 0.6. (Click a number and type, or drag it.)

    You should now see: a brown-headed Noise Texture node at the left, not yet wired to anything. The ball has not changed.

    What do Scale and Detail do?

    Scale is how many blobs fit across the object: 2 gives a few big continents, 12 gives freckles. Detail adds smaller wrinkles on top of the big blobs. Roughness is how strong those wrinkles are. The comparison pictures after Step 11 show Scale 2 and 12.

  3. A Color Ramp

    The Shader Editor. Shift+A again.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Shift+A › Color › Color Ramp. Click it down below the Principled BSDF, to the right of the Noise Texture.

    You should now see: a blue-headed Color Ramp node with a black-to-white bar across it.

    What is a Color Ramp?

    A translator. Whatever number comes in (0 to 1) picks a spot along the bar, and the colour at that spot goes out. With black at the left and white at the right it changes nothing yet; Step 11 moves the ends so it turns greys into a hard black-or-white mask.

  4. Two wires

    The sockets (dots) on the sides of the nodes.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Drag from the Noise Texture’s Fac dot (right edge) to the Color Ramp’s Fac dot (left edge). Let go on the dot.
    2. b
      Drag from the Color Ramp’s Color dot to the Mix Shader’s Factor dot. The Factor number box vanishes: a wire is deciding it now.

    You should now see: two new wires, and the ball showing soft, smeared patches of rust in Material Preview.

    I dropped the wire in the wrong place

    Wires only connect if you release exactly on a socket dot. If nothing happened, drag again. If it connected to the wrong socket, drag the wire’s end off the socket into empty space to remove it, then redo.

  5. Cut the cloud: two stops

    The Color Ramp node: the two little flags under its bar.

    Predict first: If you moved both stops to 0.20 and 0.30, would the ball be mostly rust or mostly steel?

    Do this:

    1. a
      Click the black flag at the left end of the bar. A Pos box appears below: type 0.45.
    2. b
      Click the white flag at the right end. Pos: 0.55.

    You should now see: sharp-edged rust patches on dark steel. Click the Ball in the viewport and orbit around it: the pattern wraps all the way round.

    Why 0.45 and 0.55?

    The noise cloud is mostly middle greys. Putting black at 0.45 and white at 0.55 means anything darker than 0.45 is steel, anything lighter than 0.55 is rust, and only the thin band between blends: crisp edges and about half the ball rusted. Move both stops left for more rust, right for less, further apart for softer edges. The widget above lets you try it live.

What the numbers do

End of Part 3. Save.

Part 4

Concrete, steel, dust

Tools: the Material tab again, three times.

The rest of the scene needs no nodes: three Principled BSDFs with the right three numbers each. It goes fast because the blocks already share one material, and so do the links.

Concrete (blocks)
Base Color 7A7570
Metallic 0
Roughness 0.9
Steel (chain, ball eye)
Base Color 5A5A5A
Metallic 1.0
Roughness 0.5
Ground (floor)
Base Color 888880
Metallic 0
Roughness 0.95
RustySteel (ball)
Metallic BSDF 3A3A3A, Roughness 0.65
+ Principled 8B3A1A, Metallic 0, Roughness 0.85
Noise 6 / 4 / 0.6, stops 0.45 / 0.55

  1. Concrete for all twenty blocks

    Any block, then the Material tab. Back in the Layout tab if you prefer; the Shading tab works too.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Click any block. Material tab: Brick, with a small 20 beside the name.
    2. b
      Click the name, type Concrete, Enter. Base Color › Hex 7A7570. Metallic stays 0. Roughness 0.9.

    You should now see: every block grey-brown at once.

    Why did all twenty change?

    Shift+D in Lab 1 made copies that share the original’s material. The 20 is the number of users. Editing a shared material edits it for all of them, which is exactly what you want here. The old version of this lab had you select every block and make a new material: unnecessary.

  2. Steel for the chain

    Any link, then the Material tab.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Click any link. Material: Steel, with a 6: five links plus the Ball’s eye slot.
    2. b
      Base Color › Hex 5A5A5A. Metallic 1.0. Roughness 0.5.

    You should now see: the whole chain, and the eye on the ball, turned to mid-grey metal with blurred reflections.

    Why Metallic 1.0 and not 0.8 like Lab 1?

    Real materials are either metal or not; 0.8 is a fudge that looks like neither. The dial is there for blending between two real materials with a mask, like the ball. Everything else: 0 or 1.

  3. A dusty floor

    The Ground, then the Material tab.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Click the floor. Material: Ground. Base Color › Hex 888880. Roughness 0.95. Metallic stays 0.

    You should now see: a flat, dusty grey floor with no shine.

    What does IOR do? It is in every panel.

    Index of refraction: how strongly a non-metal reflects at glancing angles. 1.5 is right for almost everything that is not metal or water, so leave it. The old sheet listed it for concrete; it was already 1.5.

End of Part 4. Save.

Part 5

Light it and render it

Tools: F12, the World tab, the light Data tab, Image › Save As.

Material Preview has been lying kindly: it lights the scene with a studio light that is not in your file. A render uses only what is in the file: one small point light and a near-black world. Two fixes make the render match.

  1. Render it once, badly

    The viewport, F12.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Hover the viewport, press F12. A render window opens and draws the frame.
    2. b
      Look at it: dark, dull, the rust barely visible. Press Esc to close the render window.

    You should now see: a dark render, nothing like the viewport.

    Why is it so different?

    The viewport in Material Preview uses a built-in HDRI studio light. Rendering uses the scene’s own world (the dark grey background colour) and its lights (one 1000 W point light, 4 m from the ball and 20 m from the wall). Checkpoint A was this picture.

  2. A brighter world

    Properties › the World tab (red globe icon).

    Do this:

    1. a
      World tab › Surface › Color: click the swatch, Hex 9FB4C8 (a pale sky grey-blue). Strength stays 1.0.

    You should now see: in Rendered shading (fourth sphere) the whole scene is lit softly from all sides and the metal reflects a pale sky.

    What is the World?

    An infinitely big sphere around everything, glowing with one colour. It is the sky: soft light from every direction, and the thing that shiny surfaces reflect. A dark world means dull metal, however good the material is.

  3. Turn the point light into a sun

    The Outliner, the green light Data tab, the sidebar.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Outliner: click Light. Properties › the green bulb tab. Under Light, click Sun. Strength: 3.
    2. b
      Sidebar (N) › Rotation: X 50, Y 10, Z -60. A sun has no position, only a direction.

    You should now see: crisp shadows from the chain and the blocks in Rendered shading; the rust patches readable.

    Why a sun?

    A point light fades with distance: 1000 W is bright next to the ball and nothing by the wall. A sun is parallel light that is the same strength everywhere, like daylight, and its Strength is in a different unit (about 3 for daylight, not watts).

  4. Render frame 56 and save the picture

    The Timeline frame box, F12, then the render window’s Image menu.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Timeline: frame box 56 (the ball in the wall). Hover the viewport, F12.
    2. b
      In the render window: Image › Save As. File Format PNG. Name it PhysicsLab2_RustMetal_YourName_render, click Save As Image.
    3. c
      Ctrl+S to save the .blend. Upload both to SEQTA.

    You should now see: a PNG in your folder matching Checkpoint E, and the .blend saved.

    Does the render window save on its own?

    No. Closing it throws the picture away. Image › Save As is the only way to keep a render, and it must be a PNG or JPEG, not the default OpenEXR-ish options: PNG is the one to pick.

End of the lab.

Part 6

Finished early? Pick one

Tools: everything above, used again.

Each one is a small experiment. Save first, then play.

Brick blocks (the old challenge, done properly)

Select four or five blocks (click, Shift-click). With one active, Material tab: click the little 20 next to Concrete. The number vanishes: the active block now has its own copy, Concrete.001. Rename it Brick, Base Color Hex 8B4A35, Roughness 0.85. Then, with those blocks still selected and the brick one active, Object › Link/Transfer Data › Link Materials (Ctrl+L) copies it to the others. Now the wall is mixed brick and concrete.

Bumpy rust

Rust is not just a colour; it is pitted. In the Shader Editor add Vector › Bump. Wire Noise Texture Fac into Bump Height, and Bump Normal into the Principled BSDF’s Normal socket (near the bottom). Strength 0.3. The rust patches now catch the light like a rough surface. Try a second Noise Texture with Scale 40 for finer pitting.

A real sky

World tab › Surface › Color: click the small dot to the left of the swatch and pick Sky Texture. Sun Elevation 35°, Sun Rotation 120°. Blender computes a real sky with a sun in it; the metal reflects clouds of colour instead of one flat tone. Lower the Strength to 0.3 if it blows out.

Two-colour rust

Rust is not one orange. Click the Color Ramp’s white stop and change its colour to dark brown 4A2410; add a third stop with the + button, drag it to 0.75, colour C4541F. Wire the ramp’s Color output into the Principled BSDF’s Base Color too (a socket can feed several wires). The mask now also paints the rust.

Scratched steel

Metallic BSDF has an Anisotropy socket. Set it to 0.6 and the highlight stretches into a line, like brushed metal. Rotate it with the Rotation socket (0.25). Compare on the chain by swapping its Principled BSDF for a Metallic BSDF.

Something’s not right

Find the problem that matches yours.

I can’t orbit (no middle mouse button)

Drag on the coloured gizmo itself to orbit. Or turn on Edit › Preferences › Input › Emulate 3 Button Mouse, then Alt + left-drag orbits.

The Material tab is empty, or has no slots

Nothing is selected, or you selected an empty or the camera. Click a mesh (the ball, a link, a block) in the viewport or the Outliner first.

I painted the eye link instead of the ball (or the ball did not change)

Wrong slot. The Ball has two: Steel (the eye) and RustySteel (the sphere). Click the second slot in the list before changing anything. If you already changed Steel, Ctrl+Z, or set it back: 5A5A5A, Metallic 1, Roughness 0.5.

The ball is black

A Mix Shader with an empty Shader row. Fill both rows (Steps 5 and 6). Also black: Factor wired but the Color Ramp has no input, or the Material Output has nothing in Surface.

The whole ball is one colour, no patches

The Color Ramp is not wired into Factor (the Factor box still shows a number), or the noise is not wired into the ramp. Check the two wires in Step 10. If the Factor box shows a number, the wire is missing.

The patches are soft and smeared

The ramp stops are still at 0 and 1. Step 11: black stop 0.45, white stop 0.55. Click each flag, then type into Pos.

It is almost all rust (or almost all steel)

Both stops are too low (all rust) or too high (all steel). Put them back to 0.45 and 0.55. Or the two shaders are in the wrong rows: steel must be the first Shader, rust the second.

The pattern is stretched into stripes

The Noise Texture is using UV coordinates and the sphere’s UVs are stretched at the poles. Add Input › Texture Coordinate and wire its Object output into the Noise Texture’s Vector socket.

Typing a Hex code does nothing

You are on the RGB or HSV tab of the picker. Click Hex first. Type the six characters without a #, then press Enter.

Shift+A does nothing in the Shader Editor

The mouse must be over the Shader Editor, not the viewport, when you press it. Also check the editor header says Object (not World) and shows the RustySteel name.

The wire goes to the wrong socket or will not connect

Release exactly on the dot. To remove a wrong wire, drag its end off the socket and drop it in empty space, or hold Ctrl and right-drag across it to cut it.

Only one block changed colour

That block has its own material (someone clicked the 20). Select all blocks with the properly-coloured one active (click it last), then Object › Link/Transfer Data › Link Materials.

The render is dark or black

Part 5: the world colour (9FB4C8, Strength 1) and the Sun (Strength 3) are not set, or the Sun is pointing the wrong way (Rotation 50, 10, -60). A black render with a bright viewport is always lighting, never materials.

The render shows the wrong frame

Set the frame box in the Timeline to 56 before F12. The render always uses the current frame.

My render disappeared when I closed the window

It was never saved. Render again (F12) and this time use the render window’s Image › Save As before closing.

The viewport is very slow in Material Preview

Twenty beveled blocks, a chain and a noise shader are fine on a school machine, but if it crawls, use Solid shading while you work and switch to Material Preview only to check.

There is no Metallic BSDF in my list

Blender 4.2 or older. Use Principled BSDF for the first shader too, with Base Color 3A3A3A, Metallic 1.0 and Roughness 0.65. Same result.

Eight quick questions

Pick an answer to lock it in. You’ll find out straight away whether you’re right.

1Which setting makes a surface reflect its own colour instead of white?

Right. Metal tints its reflections; everything else reflects white highlights.

Not quite. Metallic 1 is the metal switch: a metal’s reflections carry its own colour.

2Roughness 0.95 looks like

Right. High roughness scatters the reflection until it disappears.

Not quite. Roughness near 1 is matte: the dusty floor and the concrete.

3What does a Mix Shader’s Factor of 0.5 do?

Right. One number, the same everywhere, which is why the ball looked like brown paint.

Not quite. Factor is the blend between the first shader (0) and the second (1), applied evenly unless a texture drives it.

4In the rust recipe, what does the Noise Texture provide?

Right. It is a pattern of numbers, not a colour; the ramp turns it into a mask.

Not quite. Noise Texture outputs a grey cloud of values from 0 to 1. The Color Ramp turns it into a mask; the colours come from the two shaders.

5Moving both Color Ramp stops to 0.30 and 0.40 would make the ball

Right. Lower stops mean more of the cloud counts as white (rust).

Not quite. The cloud is mostly middle greys; cutting it lower makes more of it white, so more rust.

6The number 20 next to a material name means

Right. Users. Edit it once and all twenty change.

Not quite. It is the user count: twenty objects point at this one material.

7Why does the render look dark when Material Preview looks fine?

Right. Fix the world colour and add a sun and they match.

Not quite. Material Preview lights the scene with its own HDRI. A render only has the lights and world you set up.

8A render is kept when you

Right. Ctrl+S saves the .blend, not the picture.

Not quite. Only Image › Save As keeps a render; Ctrl+S saves the scene file, and closing the window discards the picture.

Check yourself

Tick each one you can honestly do now. Anything left unticked is what to ask about next lesson.

Think about it

A real wrecking ball rusts most where water sits and least where the chain rubs. Our noise does not know that. What node could you add so the rust is heavier near the bottom of the ball? (Hint: Input › Texture Coordinate gives you position.)

Upload to SEQTA — Physics Lab 2

Upload PhysicsLab2_RustMetal_YourName.blend and PhysicsLab2_RustMetal_YourName_render.png. The .blend should contain the RustySteel node material on the ball, Concrete on the blocks, Steel on the chain, Ground on the floor, a pale world and a sun.

Due one week from when this lab was handed out.

Teacher notes

Timing

Two lessons. Lesson 1: Parts 1–3 (the ball). Lesson 2: Parts 4–5 (the rest, lighting, render) and extensions. The start file is embedded in Step 1 for anyone without a working Lab 1 file; it is the finished Lab 1 scene with the cache baked (220 KB).

What changed from the original sheet

  • The two-slot ball. Joining the sphere into the bottom link in Lab 1 leaves the Ball with two material slots (Steel for the eye, Iron for the sphere). The original said “click on the wrecking ball (torus/sphere)” and “+ New”, which would add a third slot assigned to nothing. Step 3 selects the right slot instead.
  • Materials are shared. The original had students select every block and apply new Concrete settings, and did not say how. Shift+D copies share materials, so the blocks (20 users) and links (6) are edited once each; the user-count number is taught, and the brick variant extension shows how to make a copy deliberately.
  • Exact ramp stops (0.45 / 0.55) replace “adjust the ColorRamp stops”, with rendered comparisons for Scale 2/6/12 and three stop settings so the effect of each number is visible before touching it. Noise Scale 6 / Detail 4 / Roughness 0.6 replaces 10 / 6, which gave freckles rather than patches on a 3 m ball.
  • Lighting is a Part of its own. The original ended with “Press F12”, which produces a near-black render in the Lab 1 file (default 1000 W point light, dark world): Checkpoint A shows it. World colour + a sun light are now Steps 16–17, with the Material-Preview-versus-render difference explained, since this is the most common “my render is broken” question.
  • Editor type dropdown → Shading workspace. Switching the Timeline to a Shader Editor gives a strip too small to work in; the Shading tab is the standard route.
  • Metallic BSDF is kept (it exists from Blender 4.3) with a troubleshooting entry for older versions. IOR is explained rather than listed. “Compare with a real photo” is dropped; the think-about-it question asks for a position-driven mask instead.

Tested values

Every material was built from these steps on the Lab 1 file in Blender 5.2.2 (bpy) and rendered with EEVEE, the engine students will use; the checkpoint pictures are those renders (Hex colours entered as sRGB, as the Hex tab does). Node names (Color Ramp, Noise Texture, Mix Shader, Metallic BSDF), the Add-menu categories and the Factor socket name are as in Blender 4.3 onwards.

Where students usually get stuck

Editing the Steel slot instead of RustySteel. Leaving a Shader row on None (black ball). Releasing a wire beside the socket instead of on it. Typing Hex while on the RGB tab. Pressing Shift+A over the viewport (adds a mesh) instead of the node editor. Forgetting Image › Save As.

Quiz answers

1 Metallic 1. 2 Dusty, no highlight. 3 Blends equally everywhere. 4 A random cloud deciding where. 5 Mostly rust. 6 Twenty objects share it. 7 Studio light vs your lights. 8 Image › Save As.
